we have solved the structure of DC-SIGN in solution for the first time and have used this information to show that the binding mode of the DC-SIGNR carbohydrate recognition domain for Man9GlcNac is different to the binding modes of smaller glycans.
the C-type lectin, DC-SIGNR binds the HIV envelope glycan, Man9GlcNc2 in a different mode from that observed for smaller glycans, and that DC-SIGNRs carbohydrate recognition domain is highly dynamic.

the C-type lectin, DC-SIGNR binds the high-mannose glycan, Man9GlcNAC, from the HIV viral envelope, in a different manner to that observed in the crystallized complex with the smaller glycan, (GlcNA)2Man3.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of a new generation of drugs that can prevent the spread of HIV and other pathogens, by inhibiting the binding of viral glycans to the C-type lectin receptors that promote infection.
the development and application of novel NMR techniques to study the structure and dynamics of protein-ligand interactions, and the use of NMR to understand the molecular basis of disease.
the development and application of NMR spectroscopy to study carbohydrate-binding proteins.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the C-type lectin domain of DC-SignR has been shown to be a highly dynamic domain, with different modes of binding for different glycans, including those found on the HIV virus.

our work has provided the first structural information on DC-SIGNR interactions with the high mannose glycan Man9GlcNac, as found on HIV viral envelopes, and has provided a unique view on the binding modes of DC-SIGN with a range of glycants.

the solution-state nuclear magnetic spectroscopic data presented here provide the first insight into the binding modes of DC-SIGN to a variety of glycans, including the first structural data of the DC-SIGN carbohydrate recognition domain in complex with a disease-associated glycan, and reveal the solution dynamics of this protein.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the solution state data we have generated provide the first structural information on a C-type lectins binding to a glycan derived from the HIV viral envelope.
we have provided new insights into the binding mode for the first time of DC-SIGN with the high-mannose oligosaccharide Man9GlcNac2 derived from the gp120 envelope protein of HIV.
DC-SIGN has a different binding modes for different glycans, and the binding mode for glycane on HIV is different from that of small glycan fragments.
The main takeaway from our work is that
DC-SIGN binds to the viral envelope in a different mode than it does to the small glycans that have been previously studied in the crystalline phase.
the binding mode of DC-SIGN for the larger glycan Man9GlcNac is different from those of small glycands previously observed in crystalline state.
DC-SIGN binds Man9GlcNac derived from gp120 differently to smaller glycans, suggesting that using this glycan may provide a more selective inhibitor for DC-SIGN than smaller glycans.
